items.name: Coca-Cola bottle
clues: A sweet, fizzy drink. Most people in the world could recognise its pack with their eyes closed.
Pretty much everyone, in almost every country on Earth.
In 1915 a glass company in Indiana, USA, won a competition to design it.
Green-tinted glass with curves and ribs. The designer got the idea from a picture of a cocoa bean.
The brief said people should recognise it in the dark just by touch, or even lying broken on the ground.
A curvy glass bottle for the world's most famous cola.

items.name: Pringles
clues: Salty snacks, stacked neatly on top of each other, all exactly the same shape.
Snack lovers, party hosts, and anyone whose hand has ever got stuck at the bottom.
An American company first sold it in 1968.
A tall cardboard tube with a plastic lid. Inside, the crisps are curved like a saddle.
The chemist who designed the tube asked for some of his ashes to be buried in one, and his children did it.
Its mascot is a man with a huge moustache called Mr. P.

items.name: Kinder Surprise
clues: Chocolate on the outside, and something you definitely can't eat on the inside.
Children, and adults who collect what's inside.
An Italian family company launched it in 1974.
An egg made of milk chocolate with a white layer inside, wrapped in thin, shiny foil.
Inside there's a yellow plastic capsule with a small toy that you often have to build yourself.
In Germany it's called the Überraschungsei, or Ü-Ei.

items.name: Club-Mate
clues: A fizzy drink that tastes a bit strange the first time, a little like tea.
Berlin clubbers, computer hackers, and students in exam week.
Its recipe goes back to 1924, and today it's made by a small family brewery in Bavaria.
A glass bottle, often bought by the crate, with a drawing of a South American cowboy on the label.
Its slogan is “You'll get used to it”. It has about twice as much caffeine as cola.
It's made from yerba mate, and the first part of its name is a place where people go dancing.

items.name: Maggi Würze
clues: A few drops of a dark, salty liquid. Your grandparents probably put it in their soup.
Home cooks, especially in German-speaking countries.
A Swiss businessman launched it in 1886.
A tall, dark brown bottle with a narrow neck, so it comes out drop by drop, and a red and yellow label.
In German, a garden herb that smells just like it is nicknamed after it.
The brand name is also the surname of its founder, Julius Maggi.

items.name: Absolut
clues: A clear drink with no colour, very little smell, and quite a lot of attitude.
Party people, cocktail bars, and art fans who love its old adverts.
It was launched in Sweden in 1979.
A short glass bottle with round shoulders and no paper label: the writing is printed straight onto the glass.
The shape came from an old Swedish medicine bottle. For years its adverts were just that bottle shape, hidden in pictures.
A Swedish vodka whose name is the Swedish word for “absolute”.
